mainTopic: Craftsmen who ruin their work: betrothing with wages, the expert butcher, and the money changer's mistake
overview: The amud opens with רבא's explanation of the argument between רבי מאיר and the רבנן about a craftsman who betroths a woman with his wages. Everyone agrees that a wage is a debt and that betrothing with a debt fails. The argument is only about a case where he also added a jewel of his own: is her mind on the jewel or on the loan? The גמרא then shows that the same split appears in a three-way ברייתא of תנאים. Next, שמואל rules that an expert butcher who ruins the שחיטה must pay, even when he works for free, and explains that he follows רבי מאיר, who holds that one who stumbles is פושע. רבי יוחנן's rulings are reconciled by splitting the cases: a paid butcher pays, and an unpaid expert is exempt. After a story about רב and a badly slaughtered animal, the גמרא turns to a money changer who approves a bad coin. Only a top expert who erred on a brand-new coin is exempt. רבי חייא paid such a woman anyway, acting לפנים משורת הדין, and רב יוסף's source for this begins at the end of the amud and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבא says everyone agrees on all three earlier points
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects the earlier explanations. He holds that both sides agree that wages accrue from beginning to end, that קידושין with a loan does not work, and that a craftsman does not own the improvement to a vessel.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Everyone agrees that wages build up from the beginning of the job to the end. Everyone agrees that if a man betroths a woman with a loan, she is not betrothed. And everyone agrees that a craftsman does not acquire the improvement he makes to a vessel.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא begins a new explanation of the dispute by first removing all three earlier possible reasons for it. This clears the way for his own explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier approaches explained the argument by saying רבי מאיר and רבנן disagree on one of these three rules. רבא says they agree on all three, so the wage the craftsman earned is a plain debt, and betrothing with a debt fails. Something else must explain why רבי מאיר says she is betrothed.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees
Wages build up continuously from the start of the job to its end
One who betroths a woman with money she already owes him
A craftsman does not own the added value he gives a vessel

steps.confusionAlert: Because wages build up throughout the job, by the end the whole wage is already a debt she owes him. That is why betrothing her with it counts as betrothing with a loan.

phrases.english: Rava said:
Everyone agrees that wages are owed
from the beginning to the end,
phrases.notes: The wage builds up bit by bit all along, not all at once when the job is finished.

phrases.english: and everyone agrees that one who betroths with a loan,
she is not betrothed,
and everyone agrees that a craftsman does not
acquire the improvement of the vessel;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a new explanation of the dispute, replacing the earlier explanations discussed before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both רבי מאיר and רבנן agree that wages accrue throughout, that קידושין with a מלוה fails, and that an אומן does not acquire שבח כלי.

steps.title: The case is where he added a jewel of his own
steps.stepSummary: רבא sets the case where the craftsman added a jewel of his own. רבי מאיר holds that with a loan plus a פרוטה, she focuses on the פרוטה, so she is betrothed. רבנן hold she focuses on the loan, so she is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what case are we dealing with? A case where he added a jewel of his own for her. רבי מאיר holds that when there is a loan and a פרוטה, her mind is on the פרוטה. The רבנן hold that when there is a loan and a פרוטה, her mind is on the loan.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא now gives his own explanation. The craftsman added a small jewel of his own, and the argument is about which part of what he gave the woman is thinking of as her קידושין money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The added jewel is real new value, at least a פרוטה, so it could work as קידושין. רבי מאיר says she accepts the קידושין because of that new item, so it works. רבנן say she has the loan in mind, and קידושין with a loan fails.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (Used to narrow the case down)
A precious stone or jewel
A loan together with a פרוטה of new money or value
Her mind, what she is focused on

steps.whyThisMatters: This moves the dispute away from the three technical rules about wages and loans. It becomes a question of what the woman has in mind when she receives a mix of a debt and new value.

phrases.english: Rather, with what are we dealing here?
With a case where he added for her
a jewel of his own.
Rabbi Meir holds:
a loan and a peruta —
her mind is on the peruta,
phrases.notes: Here the jewel is the פרוטה, the new value he gave her.

phrases.english: and the Rabbis hold:
a loan and a peruta — her mind is on the loan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Having ruled out the three earlier explanations, רבא now gives the actual case and the real point of disagreement.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (אוקימתא) to a craftsman who added his own jewel
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think the dispute is about when wages accrue, about קידושין with a loan, or about the craftsman's ownership of the improvement.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dispute is whether, with a loan plus a פרוטה, the woman focuses on the פרוטה (רבי מאיר: she is betrothed) or on the loan (רבנן: she is not).

steps.title: This is the same as a dispute of תנאים: past work versus future work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says this argument matches a dispute of תנאים in a ברייתא. The first opinion says wages for past work cannot be used for קידושין, but wages for future work can. רבי נתן says neither works.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is the same as the dispute of these תנאים, as it was taught: If he says 'with the wage for the work I did for you,' she is not betrothed. If he says 'with the wage for the work I will do for you,' she is betrothed. רבי נתן says: 'with the wage for the work I will do for you,' she is not betrothed, and all the more so 'with the wage for the work I did for you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא links רבא's dispute to an older argument among תנאים and begins quoting the ברייתא. This step brings the first two opinions. The third opinion, which contains the key line, comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wages for past work are already a debt, so all opinions agree that this is קידושין with a loan, which fails. The first opinion holds that future work is different and does work for קידושין. רבי נתן holds that wages build up during the job, so even future work ends up being a debt, and it fails too.

keyTerms.meaning: It is the same as the dispute of these תנאים
With the wage for the work I already did for you
With the wage for the work I will do for you
All the more so

phrases.english: And it is the same as the dispute of these Tannaim,
as it was taught:
"With the wage for the work I did for you" —
phrases.notes: He means: be betrothed to me with this. She already owes him that wage, so it is a loan.

phrases.english: she is not betrothed.
"With the wage for the work I will do for you" — she is betrothed.
Rabbi Natan says:
"With the wage for the work I will do for you" — she is not betrothed,
and all the more so "with the wage for the work I did for you."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the dispute רבא described already appears among the תנאים.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's explanation that the dispute is about a loan plus an added פרוטה (jewel)
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא with a three-way dispute about betrothing with wages for past or future work

steps.title: רבי יהודה הנשיא: adding a jewel makes the betrothal work
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה הנשיא says that with wages, whether for past or future work, she is not betrothed. But if he added a jewel of his own, she is betrothed. This is exactly the case רבא described.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה הנשיא says: In truth they said: whether 'with the wage for the work I did for you' or 'with the wage for the work I will do for you,' she is not betrothed. But if he added a jewel of his own for her, she is betrothed.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends with רבי יהודה הנשיא's opinion, which brings up the very case of an added jewel. This shows that תנאים already argued about רבא's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה הנשיא agrees that the wage by itself is only a loan and cannot betroth. But once new value is added, he holds she is betrothed. That is the view רבא gave to רבי מאיר, that her mind is on the פרוטה. As Step 6 will show, רבי נתן disagrees on this point, which matches the view of the רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: In truth they said, used to introduce a firm, accepted rule
Whether... or...
He added a jewel of his own for her

steps.whatToRemember: רבא: everyone agrees that wages are a debt and that betrothing with a debt fails. The only argument is when he adds a jewel. רבי מאיר says her mind is on the new item, so she is betrothed. רבנן say her mind is on the loan, so she is not. רבי יהודה הנשיא in the ברייתא holds like רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says,
in truth they said:
whether "with the wage for the work I did for you,"
or "with the wage for the work I will do for you" —
she is not betrothed.
But if he added a jewel of his own for her —
she is betrothed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הַנָּשִׂיא אוֹמֵר, בֶּאֱמֶת אָמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא with the opinion that matches רבא's added-jewel case.
steps.raayaObject: That the added-jewel case is an older dispute among תנאים
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יהודה הנשיא's ruling in the ברייתא that an added נופך makes the betrothal work

steps.title: What separates the תנא קמא from רבי נתן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the practical difference is between the תנא קמא and רבי נתן. It answers that they argue about when wages become owed (שכירות).
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between the first תנא and רבי נתן? The difference between them is about wages.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the first two opinions in the ברייתא really differ, and answers in one word: wages (שכירות).
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא allowed קידושין with wages for future work, but רבי נתן did not. The reason is that they argue about when wages become owed. If wages are owed only at the end, the future payment is fresh money and the קידושין works. If wages build up from the start, the payment is really paying off a loan, and קידושין with a loan does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: The first, unnamed opinion in a משנה or ברייתא
What is the practical difference between them?
Wages; here, the question of when a worker's pay becomes owed

phrases.aramaic: מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין תַּנָּא קַמָּא לְרַבִּי נָתָן?
phrases.english: What is the difference between the first tanna and Rabbi Natan?
phrases.notes: This goes back to the ברייתא from Step 3: the first opinion allowed future wages for קידושין, and רבי נתן did not.

phrases.english: The difference between them is wages.
phrases.notes: He means: do wages become owed bit by bit from the start, or only at the end of the job?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין תַּנָּא קַמָּא לְרַבִּי נָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Breaks down the three-way dispute brought in Steps 3 and 4, starting with the first two opinions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What practical issue separates the תנא קמא from רבי נתן?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They argue about שכירות: whether wages become owed only at the end or bit by bit from the beginning.

steps.title: What separates רבי נתן from רבי יהודה הנשיא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the difference is between רבי נתן and רבי יהודה הנשיא. It answers that they argue about a loan plus a פרוטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between רבי נתן and רבי יהודה הנשיא? The difference between them is a loan plus a פרוטה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains how the second and third opinions differ: they argue about a loan together with a פרוטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the craftsman adds a jewel of his own, the woman receives both the wages (which count as a loan) and something new, the jewel. רבי נתן holds that she is focused on the loan, so she is not betrothed. רבי יהודה הנשיא holds that she is focused on the פרוטה, meaning the jewel, so she is betrothed. This is the same split רבא described between רבי מאיר and רבנן in Step 2.

keyTerms.meaning: A loan; money already owed to her
The smallest coin of value, the minimum needed for קידושין

steps.whatToRemember: Three opinions, two arguments: the תנא קמא and רבי נתן argue about when wages become owed, and רבי נתן and רבי יהודה הנשיא argue about a loan plus a פרוטה. This matches רבא's explanation exactly.

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין רַבִּי נָתָן לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הַנָּשִׂיא?
phrases.english: And between Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi?
The difference between them is a loan and a peruta.
phrases.notes: The wages count as the loan, and the jewel he added counts as the פרוטה.

steps.triggerLanguage: בֵּין רַבִּי נָתָן לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הַנָּשִׂיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the breakdown of the ברייתא, showing it matches רבא's explanation.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What practical issue separates רבי נתן from רבי יהודה הנשיא?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They argue about מלוה ופרוטה: is her mind focused on the loan or on the פרוטה (the jewel)?

steps.title: שמואל: an expert butcher who ruins an animal must pay
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that an expert טבח who slaughters incorrectly and makes the animal unkosher must pay. His reasons are that he is a מזיק and a פושע, like someone told to slaughter in one spot who slaughtered in another.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: An expert butcher who ruined an animal must pay. He is a damager, he is negligent, and he is treated like someone who was told 'slaughter for me from here' and slaughtered from somewhere else.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the main topic of a craftsman who damages what he works on. שמואל rules that an expert טבח who ruins the slaughter must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think an expert who made an honest mistake is excused. שמואל says no: he caused the damage (מזיק) and he was careless (פושע). He is like a worker who went against the owner's clear instructions, because the owner obviously wanted a kosher slaughter.

keyTerms.meaning: A butcher, here one who does the שחיטה
An expert, a trained professional
Ruined it; here, made the animal unkosher
One who causes damage
Negligent, careless

phrases.english: Shmuel said: An expert butcher who ruined [the animal]
is liable to pay.
He is a damager; he is negligent;
he is like one to whom [the owner] said: 'Slaughter for me from here,'
and he slaughtered for him from there.
phrases.notes: The second 'from here' means a different spot from the one he was told, so he went against the owner's wishes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the קידושין discussion and returns to the topic of a craftsman who damages what he works on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An expert טבח who makes an animal unkosher must pay, because he is a מזיק and a פושע, like one who disobeyed the owner's instructions.

steps.title: Why did שמואל need both reasons
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why שמואל said both 'he is a מזיק' and 'he is a פושע'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why did he need to say both 'he is a damager' and 'he is negligent'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why שמואל gave two reasons when one seems like enough. It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word in a teaching should add something. If 'מזיק' already makes him pay, the extra word 'פושע' must be teaching a new case.

keyTerms.meaning: Why did he need to say it? (asking about extra words)

phrases.aramaic: לְמָה לֵיהּ לְמֵימַר ״מַזִּיק הוּא, פּוֹשֵׁעַ הוּא״?
phrases.english: Why does he need to say 'he is a damager, he is negligent'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks closely at the wording of שמואל's statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does each of the two reasons, מזיק and פושע, add?

steps.title: פושע teaches that even an unpaid butcher pays
steps.stepSummary: Had שמואל said only 'מזיק', we would think he pays only when working for pay. 'פושע' teaches that even when working for free he must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he had said only 'he is a damager,' I would have thought this applies only when he works for pay, but not when he works for free. So he tells us 'he is negligent.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word 'פושע' is there to include a butcher who works for free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'מזיק' alone might suggest the strict liability that comes from taking money for the job. 'פושע' shows the problem is carelessness, and even someone doing a free favor must pay for carelessness. So the rule covers both the paid and the unpaid butcher.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have thought (an idea that turns out to be wrong)
For pay
For free
He teaches us (the new point)

phrases.english: If he had said [only] 'he is a damager,'
I would have said: these words apply
where he does it for pay,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הֵיכָא דְּקָא עָבֵיד בְּחִנָּם – לָא;
phrases.english: but where he does it for free, no;
so he teaches us 'he is negligent.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'מזיק' alone might be limited to a paid butcher; 'פושע' extends liability to one who works for free.

steps.title: רב חמא בר גוריא challenges שמואל from a ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רב חמא בר גוריא quotes a ברייתא: an unpaid expert butcher who ruins an animal is exempt, while an ordinary person is liable, and if paid, both are liable. This seems to contradict שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חמא בר גוריא challenged שמואל: If someone gives an animal to a butcher and he makes it unkosher, an expert is exempt and an ordinary person is liable. And if he is paid, both the ordinary person and the expert are liable!
steps.whatsHappening: רב חמא בר גוריא brings a ברייתא that seems to say an unpaid expert butcher does not pay, which goes against שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל just said even an unpaid expert must pay. The ברייתא says an expert is liable only when paid, so an unpaid expert is exempt. This hits the exact case Step 9 added.

keyTerms.meaning: Made it a נבלה, an animal that died without valid שחיטה
An ordinary person, not an expert
Exempt, does not have to pay

phrases.aramaic: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא לִשְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: Rav Ḥama bar Gurya challenged Shmuel:
One who gives an animal to a butcher, and he made it a carcass:
an expert is exempt; an ordinary person is liable.
And if he gives payment,
whether ordinary or expert, he is liable!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיתִיבֵיהּ רַב חָמָא בַּר גּוּרְיָא לִשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks שמואל's rule, especially the unpaid case added in Step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that an expert טבח pays even when working for free.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא makes the expert liable only when paid, which implies an unpaid expert is exempt, against שמואל.

steps.title: שמואל sharply dismisses the challenge
steps.stepSummary: שמואל answers with a sharp rebuke: 'May your mind be muddled!' He treats the challenge as not worth taking seriously.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: May your mind be muddled!
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל does not accept the challenge. He waves it away with a sharp remark, showing he thinks the question misses the point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here שמואל does not explain why the ברייתא does not disprove him. His harsh words only show that he sees no real contradiction, without saying here how the ברייתא fits.

keyTerms.meaning: May your mind be muddled (a sharp rebuke)

phrases.english: He said to him: May your mind be muddled!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: שמואל's reaction to רב חמא בר גוריא's challenge.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the whole challenge from the ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Not stated in this line; שמואל only signals that he thinks the challenge is mistaken.

steps.title: A second scholar raises the same objection
steps.stepSummary: Another scholar comes and challenges שמואל with the same ברייתא that רב חמא בר גוריא used.
steps.simpleTranslation: One of the Sages came and raised the same objection against him.
steps.whatsHappening: A different scholar challenges שמואל again with the same ברייתא. This sets up שמואל's real answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Last time שמואל only brushed the question off with a rebuke. Now the same challenge comes back. This time שמואל will give an actual reason why the ברייתא is no problem for him.

keyTerms.meaning: one of the Sages / scholars
raises an objection

phrases.english: A certain one of the Sages came
and raised an objection against him.
phrases.notes: It is the same objection from the ברייתא in Step 10.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתָא הָהוּא מֵרַבָּנַן קָא מוֹתֵיב לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the challenge of Step 10 after שמואל's brush-off in Step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that an expert טבח who ruins an animal must pay, even when he works for free.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says an unpaid expert is exempt, so it seems to contradict שמואל.

steps.title: שמואל explains that his ruling follows רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: שמואל scolds the scholar and explains that his ruling follows רבי מאיר, while the ברייתא follows the רבנן. His own wording proves this.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Now you will get what your friend got! I am telling you the view of רבי מאיר, and you answer me with the view of the רבנן?! Why did you not look carefully at my words? I said: he is a מזיק, he is a פושע, he is like someone told 'slaughter for me from here' who slaughtered from there. Who holds this reasoning? רבי מאיר, who says: he should have taken the responsibility on himself!
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל finally answers the challenge. He says his ruling follows רבי מאיר, and the ברייתא follows the רבנן, who disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no contradiction. The ברייתא is simply the other side of a מחלוקת. שמואל proves he follows רבי מאיר from his own comparison to a person who slaughtered in the wrong spot. That idea, 'he should have taken the responsibility on himself,' is רבי מאיר's reasoning.

keyTerms.meaning: now you will get (the same scolding)
you did not look carefully at my words
reasoning, logic
he should have taken the responsibility on himself

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל follows רבי מאיר: someone who takes on a job must carry the responsibility for doing it right. The ברייתא that exempts the unpaid expert follows the רבנן.
steps.confusionAlert: שמואל is not saying the ברייתא is wrong. He is saying it follows a different תנא (the רבנן), so it cannot be used to challenge a ruling that follows רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: He said to him: Now you will receive
what your friend received!
phrases.notes: He means the scolding he gave רב חמא בר גוריא in Step 11.

phrases.english: I am telling you the view of Rabbi Meir,
and you answer me with the Rabbis?!
Why did you not look carefully at my words?

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֲנִי אוֹמֵר: מַזִּיק הוּא, פּוֹשֵׁעַ הוּא,
phrases.english: For I say: He is a damager, he is negligent,
he is like one who was told 'Slaughter for me from here'
and he slaughtered it from there;
Who holds this reasoning?
Rabbi Meir, who says:
He should have taken it upon himself!

steps.triggerLanguage: קָאָמֵינָא לְכוּ אֲנָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר, וְקָאָמְרִיתוּ לִי רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection raised in Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigning the opinions to different תנאים: שמואל follows רבי מאיר, and the ברייתא follows the רבנן.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to be an accepted ruling that disproves שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is the רבנן's view. שמואל holds like רבי מאיר, who makes the person who took on the job responsible for it.
steps.whyThisMatters: It explains why שמואל chose the comparison to slaughtering in the wrong spot: that wording points to רבי מאיר's reasoning.

steps.title: Which ruling of רבי מאיר does שמואל mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which statement of רבי מאיר holds this idea. It first suggests the משנה about an owner who tied up his ox properly and is still liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which ruling of רבי מאיר? If we say it is this one of רבי מאיר (the memory aid is קל״ן), as we learned in a משנה: if the owner tied his ox with reins or locked the gate in front of it properly, and it got out and caused damage, whether it is a תם or a מועד, he is liable. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where רבי מאיר teaches this idea. It offers a first suggestion: the משנה where an owner who guarded his ox properly still has to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the owner took normal care, רבי מאיר still makes him liable. That looks like the same idea: someone who has a responsibility must fully carry it. The word אילימא tells us this suggestion is about to be rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: which?
if you say (a suggestion that will be rejected)
memory aid
reins, a strap for tying
an ox not known to cause damage
an ox known (forewarned) to cause damage

phrases.english: Which ruling of Rabbi Meir?
If we say this one of Rabbi Meir,
phrases.notes: Some versions don't have the word in square brackets.

phrases.english: (the memory aid is: ק-ל-ן)
phrases.notes: A memory aid for the three rulings of רבי מאיר the גמרא will bring: tied (קשרו), to dye (לצבוע), broke (נשברה).

phrases.english: As we learned: If its owner tied it with reins
or locked the gate before it properly,
and it got out and caused damage,
whether innocuous or forewarned, he is liable,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר? אִילֵּימָא הָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks for the source of the רבי מאיר opinion that שמואל relied on in Step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which ruling of רבי מאיר holds that someone who takes on a responsibility is liable even if he was not careless on purpose?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: First suggestion: the משנה of the tied ox. It will be rejected in the next step.

steps.title: The tied-ox case is about reading פסוקים, not logic
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion: in the tied-ox משנה, the disagreement comes from how to read פסוקים, so it cannot be the source for שמואל's logic.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, they disagree about verses!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the tied-ox משנה as the source. רבי מאיר's ruling there comes from reading פסוקים, not from the idea that a person must take on the responsibility.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל needs a ruling built on reasoning: one who takes on a task is responsible for it. In the ox case, רבי מאיר's ruling comes from how he reads the פסוקים, so we cannot carry it over to a butcher. The search for the right רבי מאיר continues.

keyTerms.meaning: there (in that case)
פסוקים, verses
they disagree

phrases.english: There, they disagree about verses!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the source suggested in Step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the tied-ox משנה as the source. רבי מאיר's view itself is not rejected.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: That ruling comes from reading פסוקים about guarding an ox, not from general reasoning about taking on responsibility, so it cannot be applied to the butcher.

steps.title: Second suggestion: the dyer who used the wrong color
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that שמואל meant רבי מאיר's ruling in the dyer משנה, where a dyer who used the wrong color pays for the wool.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, שמואל meant this statement of רבי מאיר, as we learned in a משנה: If someone gave wool to a dyer to dye it red and he dyed it black, or black and he dyed it red, רבי מאיר says the dyer gives the owner the value of his wool.
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting the tied-ox משנה, the גמרא offers a new possible source for שמואל: the dyer who used the wrong color.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this משנה, a worker who did the job wrong has to pay, according to רבי מאיר. That looks like שמואל's idea that a worker who ruins a job is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. Introduces a new suggestion after the last one failed
To dye
A dyer
The value of his wool

phrases.english: Rather, it is this statement of Rabbi Meir
as we learned: if he gave wool to dye red for him
phrases.notes: The dyer case is a משנה a little later in this פרק, on דף ק׳.

phrases.english: and he dyed it black,
or to dye it black, and he dyed it red,
Rabbi Meir says:
he gives him the value of his wool.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the tied-ox suggestion that was rejected in Step 15 with a new candidate source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is רבי מאיר in the dyer משנה, where the dyer pays the value of the wool.

steps.title: Rejected: the dyer ruined the wool with his own hands
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the dyer case. There the dyer directly ruined the wool with his own hands, which is a different kind of case.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he ruined it and took it away from the owner with his own hands!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the dyer suggestion and says it does not prove שמואל's point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dyer directly did the wrong thing to the wool with his own hands, so of course he pays. That says nothing about whether an expert who makes an honest mistake counts as careless, which is what שמואל needs.

keyTerms.meaning: There, in that case
With his hands. Direct action
He burned it, meaning he ruined it

phrases.english: There, with his hands he burned it away from him!
phrases.notes: Literally 'burned.' He means the dyer ruined the owner's wool by his own direct action.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion in Step 16.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The dyer משנה cannot serve as the source for שמואל.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The dyer's liability comes from directly ruining the wool with his own hands, not from the idea that an expert's honest mistake counts as carelessness.

steps.title: Third suggestion: the broken jug and the fallen camel
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the ברייתא where someone's jug broke or camel fell in the road. רבי מאיר says he pays for the damage, while the חכמים say he is exempt in human court but liable by the laws of Heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, שמואל meant this statement of רבי מאיר, as we learned: If someone's jug broke and he did not remove it, or his camel fell and he did not stand it up, רבי מאיר says he is liable for the damage they cause. The חכמים say he is exempt by human law but liable by the laws of Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a third possible source for שמואל: a person whose jug broke or whose camel fell in the road.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here רבי מאיר makes a person pay even though the damage started from an accident (the jug broke, the camel fell). The חכמים disagree in human court. This sets up the explanation in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: His jug
His camel
Exempt by human (court) law
Liable by the laws of Heaven. He has a moral duty to pay, but a court cannot force him

phrases.english: Rather, it is this statement of Rabbi Meir, as we learned:
If his jug broke and he did not remove it,
or his camel fell and he did not stand it up,
Rabbi Meir says: he is liable for their damage,
and the Rabbis say: he is exempt by human law,
but liable by the laws of Heaven.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר – דִּתְנַן: נִשְׁבְּרָה כַּדּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the dyer suggestion was rejected, the גמרא offers a new candidate source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The source is רבי מאיר in the broken jug and fallen camel case.

steps.title: Their argument is whether one who stumbles is careless
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue about whether someone who stumbles counts as careless (פושע). That matches שמואל's ruling, so this is the source.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we hold that they argue about whether one who stumbles is careless.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows why the jug-and-camel case fits שמואל, and this ends the search for רבי מאיר's source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר holds that one who stumbles is פושע, because he should have watched where he was going. In the same way, an expert butcher who slips and ruins the שחיטה counts as careless and must pay, just as שמואל ruled.

keyTerms.meaning: And we hold. An accepted understanding
One who stumbles
Careless, negligent
They disagree

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל's ruling follows רבי מאיר, who holds that one who stumbles is פושע. An expert's slip still counts as carelessness, so the expert butcher pays.

phrases.english: And we hold
that they disagree about whether one who stumbles is negligent.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְקַיְימָא לַן דִּבְנִתְקַל פּוֹשֵׁעַ הוּא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the suggestion in Step 18 succeeds where the earlier ones failed.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי מאיר's view that one who stumbles is פושע is the source for שמואל's ruling that an expert butcher who ruins the שחיטה is liable.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: even a top expert butcher who ruins the slaughter pays
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה reports that רבי יוחנן says an expert butcher who ruins the שחיטה is liable, even if he is as skilled as the butchers of ציפורי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said in the name of רבי יוחנן: An expert butcher who ruined the slaughter is liable, even if he is as expert as the butchers of ציפורי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement from רבי יוחנן about the expert butcher.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן agrees that even a top expert pays when he ruins the שחיטה and makes the animal not kosher. Being highly skilled does not turn his mistake into an accident.

keyTerms.meaning: An expert butcher
Who ruined. Here, ruined the שחיטה so the animal is not kosher
The butchers of ציפורי, known as very skilled

phrases.english: Rabba bar bar Ḥana said
that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
An expert butcher who ruined the slaughter is liable,
even if he is as expert as the butchers of Tzippori.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from שמואל's source to רבי יוחנן's ruling on the same case of the expert butcher.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An expert butcher who ruins the שחיטה is liable, no matter how skilled he is.

steps.title: Contradiction: רבי יוחנן was ready to exempt an expert
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges this. רבה בר בר חנה himself told of a case before רבי יוחנן where רבי יוחנן told a butcher to prove he was an expert so he could exempt him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבי יוחנן really say this? But רבה בר בר חנה said: There was a case before רבי יוחנן in the synagogue of מעון, and he said to the butcher: Go bring proof that you are an expert at slaughtering chickens, and I will exempt you!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that רבי יוחנן seems to contradict himself about the expert butcher.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ruling, an expert pays. In the story, being an expert would get the butcher exempted. Both reports come from the same person, רבה בר בר חנה, so the contradiction is sharp.

keyTerms.meaning: And did he really say? Opens a challenge
An incident, a real case
A synagogue
And I will exempt you

phrases.english: And did Rabbi Yoḥanan say this?!
But didn't Rabba bar bar Ḥana say:
There was an incident before Rabbi Yoḥanan
in the synagogue of Maon,
and he said to him: Go bring proof
that you are an expert at slaughtering chickens,
and I will exempt you!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ruling in Step 20 using a story about רבי יוחנן.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling that an expert butcher who ruins the שחיטה is liable.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the מעון story, רבי יוחנן would exempt a butcher who proved he was an expert, which contradicts making even a top expert pay.

steps.title: Answer: free work versus paid work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that there is no contradiction. A butcher who works for free is exempt, while a paid butcher is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. Here it was for free, and there it was for pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction by saying the two rulings deal with two different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The butcher in the מעון story worked for free, so if he was an expert he could be exempt. The ruling that even an expert pays is about a butcher who was paid for the job.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. There is no contradiction
For free
For pay

steps.confusionAlert: Being an expert alone does not exempt the butcher. He is exempt only if he is an expert who also worked for free. A paid expert still pays.

phrases.english: It is not difficult;
here, it was for free; there, it was for pay.
phrases.notes: The story in מעון was a butcher working for free. The ruling that he pays is about a butcher who was paid.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא; כָּאן בְּחִנָּם, כָּאן בְּשָׂכָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in Step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): free work versus paid work.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed רבי יוחנן gave two opposite rulings on the same expert butcher.
steps.terutzMaskana: An expert butcher working for free is exempt. A paid butcher is liable even if he is an expert.

steps.title: רבי זירא's advice: pay the butcher a דינר up front
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא backs up the free/paid split with רבי זירא's advice: if you want the butcher to be responsible, pay him a דינר in advance.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what רבי זירא said: One who wants a butcher to be liable to him should pay him a דינר in advance.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support from רבי זירא for the answer it just gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא's advice only makes sense if payment is what makes the butcher responsible. Once he is paid, he must cover any damage if he ruins the שחיטה.

keyTerms.meaning: Like that which he said. Brings a supporting statement
He should pay in advance
A דינר, a coin

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a practical rule: paying the butcher is what makes him responsible for a ruined שחיטה.

phrases.english: This is like what Rabbi Zeira said:
One who wants a butcher to be liable to him
should pay him a dinar in advance.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the free/paid answer in Step 22.
steps.raayaObject: The split that a paid butcher is liable and a free one is exempt.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי זירא's advice to pay the butcher a דינר in advance so that he will be liable.

steps.title: A ברייתא makes a ruining craftsman liable as if he were paid
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: a miller, baker or butcher who ruins the work is liable 'because he is like a paid watchman.' This seems to say that even an unpaid worker is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged this: If someone brings wheat to be ground and the miller did not wet it, so it turned into bran or coarse bran; or flour to a baker who made crumbly bread; or an animal to a butcher who made it a נבלה, the worker is liable, because he is like a paid watchman!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from step 22, which said a butcher who works for free is exempt. A ברייתא seems to make a craftsman liable even without pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key word is 'like' (כְּ) a paid watchman. That word suggests the worker was not really paid but is treated as if he were. If so, even a free butcher would be liable, which goes against the split in step 22.

keyTerms.meaning: Bran and coarse bran, the husks left over instead of good flour
Crumbly, badly baked bread that falls apart
He made it a נבלה, an animal not slaughtered properly
A paid watchman, who carries more responsibility

steps.confusionAlert: The whole challenge rests on one letter: כְּנוֹשֵׂא שָׂכָר means 'LIKE a paid watchman,' which hints that he was not actually paid.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
One who brings wheat to be ground –
and the miller did not wet them,
phrases.notes: Grain was dampened before grinding so it would grind properly. Skipping that ruins it.

phrases.english: and he turned them into bran or coarse bran;
flour to the baker – and he made it into crumbly bread;
an animal to the butcher – and he made it a נבלה;
he is liable, because he is like a paid watchman!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the free/paid split that steps 22-23 set up and supported.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim from step 22 that a butcher who works for free is exempt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says the worker is liable because he is 'like' a paid watchman. That implies he was not truly paid, so even a free worker would be liable.

steps.title: Read it as 'because he IS a paid watchman'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא fixes the wording of the ברייתא: it means the worker actually was paid, so it is no proof against exempting a free butcher.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: because he is a paid watchman.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by changing one word in the ברייתא. The worker in the ברייתא really was paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once 'like a paid watchman' becomes 'a paid watchman,' the ברייתא only talks about paid craftsmen. That fits perfectly with step 22: paid is liable, free is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Say (read the text this way instead)

steps.whatToRemember: The free/paid split stands: an expert who ruins the work while being paid is liable, and an expert who does it for free is exempt.

phrases.english: Say instead: because he is a paid watchman.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the wording of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא treats even an unpaid craftsman as if he were paid.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא talks about a craftsman who was actually paid, so the free butcher is still exempt.

steps.title: רב rules on a badly slaughtered animal, and two rabbis comment
steps.stepSummary: An animal cut in the wrong spot came before רב. He declared it טריפה and exempted the butcher. רב כהנא and רב אסי told the owner, 'רב did two things to you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain animal that was cut off the proper place on the neck came before רב. He declared it טריפה and exempted the butcher from paying its value. רב כהנא and רב אסי met that man and said to him: רב did two things to you.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story about a butcher case. It ends with an unclear comment, 'two things,' which the גמרא will try to explain next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two rulings came out of רב's decision: the meat may not be eaten, and the butcher does not have to pay. The comment 'רב did two things to you' does not say whether these were good or bad for the owner, which sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal cut in the wrong spot, not in the proper place on the neck
Not kosher, may not be eaten
He exempted him (from paying)
Two (two things)

phrases.english: A certain animal cut off the proper place came before רב,
he declared it טריפה, and exempted the butcher from paying its value.

phrases.aramaic: פְּגַעוּ בֵּיהּ רַב כָּהֲנָא וְרַב אַסִּי בְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא,
phrases.english: רב כהנא and רב אסי met that man,
phrases.notes: 'That man' is the owner of the animal.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: עֲבֵיד בָּךְ רַב תַּרְתֵּי.
phrases.english: they said to him: רב did two things to you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the free/paid discussion to a story of an actual butcher case before רב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב declared the badly cut animal טריפה and exempted the butcher from paying.

steps.title: What were the 'two things'? Perhaps two rulings against the owner
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'two things' means and suggests both rulings hurt the owner: רב could have declared the animal kosher like רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה, and even according to the רבנן he should have made the butcher pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are the two? If you say two things to his loss: he should have declared it kosher like רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה, yet he declared it טריפה like the רבנן; and even if he rules like the רבנן, he should have made the butcher liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the two rabbis meant, and starts trying out one explanation: two rulings that went against the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Loss one: רב followed the stricter view of the רבנן and forbade the meat, when there was a lenient view that permits it. Loss two: once the meat was forbidden, the owner lost his money, yet רב did not make the butcher pay. This explanation is only a suggestion, and the גמרא will challenge it next.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a suggestion that may be rejected)
For the worse, to his loss
To declare it kosher
The Sages, the majority opinion

phrases.english: What are the two?
If you say two things to his loss –

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִיבְּעִי לֵיהּ לְאַכְשׁוֹרֵי כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: that he should have declared it kosher like רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה,
and instead he declared it טריפה like the רבנן;
and even if he rules like the רבנן –
he should have made the butcher liable;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what the unclear comment at the end of step 26 means, and offers a first explanation.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What 'two things' רב כהנא and רב אסי meant that רב did to the owner.

steps.title: A judge may not reveal that he disagreed with the court
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the 'two losses' reading: רב כהנא and רב אסי would not tell the owner that רב ruled against him wrongly. A ברייתא forbids a judge from revealing the court's inner disagreements, calling it gossip.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is it allowed to say something like this?! Isn't it taught: When a judge leaves court, he should not say, 'I found you innocent and my colleagues found you liable, but what can I do, since my colleagues outnumbered me.' About this it is said: 'One who goes about as a talebearer reveals secrets!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the explanation from step 27. Telling the owner that רב ruled against him unfairly would be forbidden talebearing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא teaches that a judge may not tell a litigant behind the scenes that he disagreed with the ruling. Criticizing רב's ruling to the owner is the same kind of forbidden talk. So רב כהנא and רב אסי could not have meant 'two losses,' and the גמרא will need another explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: Finds innocent
Find liable
A talebearer, one who spreads private matters

steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא is a lasting rule for judges: once a court rules, a judge who disagreed must keep the debate private and not undermine the ruling.

phrases.aramaic: וּמִי שְׁרֵי לְמֵימַר כִּי הַאי גַּוְנָא?!
phrases.english: But is it allowed to say something like this?!
But isn't it taught: when he goes out, he should not say:
phrases.notes: 'He' is a judge leaving the courthouse after the ruling.

phrases.english: 'I found you innocent and my colleagues found you liable,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מָה אֶעֱשֶׂה שֶׁחֲבֵירַי רַבּוּ עָלַי״,
phrases.english: but what can I do, since my colleagues outnumbered me,'
and about this it is said:
'One who goes about as a talebearer reveals secrets!'
phrases.notes: משלי 11:13

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי שְׁרֵי לְמֵימַר כִּי הַאי גַּוְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the 'two losses' explanation suggested in step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that 'two things' meant two rulings that hurt the owner.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Telling a litigant that the ruling against him was wrong is forbidden talebearing, as the ברייתא teaches. רב כהנא and רב אסי would not have said that, so the explanation cannot be right.

steps.title: The two things were favors, not losses
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא and רב אסי meant that רב did two good things for the owner: kept him from eating something that might be forbidden, and kept him from taking money that might not be his.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, they meant two good things: רב did not let you eat something that might be forbidden, and he kept you from money that might be stolen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new meaning to 'רב did two things to you.' The two things were helpful to the owner, not harmful.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 28 showed the rabbis would never tell the owner that רב ruled against him wrongly. So the line must be praise. The animal is in doubt, so declaring it טריפה keeps the owner from a possible איסור. Since it might really be kosher, making the butcher pay could mean the owner takes money he is not owed, which is possible גזילה.

keyTerms.meaning: two things for the good
something that might be forbidden
money that might be stolen

steps.whatToRemember: 'רב did two things to you' means two favors: no doubtful forbidden food, and no doubtful stolen money.

phrases.english: Rather, they meant two things for your good:
that he did not feed you something that might be forbidden,
and he kept you away from money that might be stolen.
phrases.notes: If the animal was really kosher, the butcher would owe nothing, so taking his money could be robbery.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem in step 28 by changing the 'two losses' reading into 'two favors'.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'two things' were two rulings that hurt the owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: The 'two things' were two favors: no doubtful איסור and no doubtful גזילה.

steps.title: Two teachings argue about a money changer's mistake
steps.stepSummary: Someone shows a coin to a money changer, who says it is good, but it turns out bad. One ברייתא says an expert is exempt; another says even an expert must pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: if a person shows a dinar to a money changer and it turns out to be bad, one ברייתא says an expert is exempt and an ordinary person is liable. Another ברייתא says both an expert and an ordinary person are liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new case about an expert who makes a mistake, and shows two ברייתות that seem to contradict each other. This sets up רב פפא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both ברייתות agree an ordinary person who misjudges the coin must pay. They argue only about the expert: one exempts him, the other makes him pay. The question is how both can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: money changer, a person who checks and exchanges coins
an expert or professional
an ordinary person, not an expert
one teaching says... and another teaching says (a contradiction)

steps.confusionAlert: Both teachings agree an ordinary person pays. The only argument is about the expert.

phrases.english: It was stated: one who shows a dinar to a money changer
and it turns out to be bad,
one teaching says: an expert is exempt,
an ordinary person is liable;
and another teaching says:
whether expert or ordinary person, he is liable!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנֵי חֲדָא: אוּמָּן – פָּטוּר, הֶדְיוֹט – חַיָּיב; וְתַנְיָא אִידַּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about an expert's mistake, related to the butcher discussion before it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two ברייתות about a money changer's liability
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One ברייתא exempts the expert and the other makes him liable, so they seem to contradict.

steps.title: רב פפא: only the top experts are exempt
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the ברייתא that exempts an expert means a top expert like דנכו and איסור, who need no more learning at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: when it teaches that an expert is exempt, it means someone like דנכו and איסור, who do not need to learn anything more.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא settles the contradiction by saying the two ברייתות talk about different levels of expert.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא that exempts the expert means only a top expert who knows everything about coins. The ברייתא that makes even an expert pay means a regular expert who still has more to learn. So there is no real argument.

keyTerms.meaning: names of two famous money changers
to learn

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כִּי תַּנְיָא אוּמָּן פָּטוּר –
phrases.english: רב פפא said: when it teaches that an expert is exempt,
it means someone like דנכו and איסור,
phrases.notes: These are two famous money changers, used here as the model of a top expert.

phrases.english: who do not need to learn at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כִּי תַּנְיָא אוּמָּן פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction from step 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (two kinds of expert)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות argue about any expert.
steps.terutzMaskana: A top expert who needs no more learning is exempt; a regular expert pays.

steps.title: How could such experts make a mistake?
steps.stepSummary: If דנכו and איסור know everything, how could they get a coin wrong?
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, what did they make a mistake about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a quick question about רב פפא's answer. It is setting up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב פפא described experts who need no more learning. Such people should never mistake a bad coin for a good one. So what kind of mistake could they make?

keyTerms.meaning: what did they make a mistake about?

phrases.english: But what did they make a mistake about?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how רב פפא's top experts could make a mistake at all.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of mistake a top expert could make.

steps.title: They erred on a brand-new coin
steps.stepSummary: The top experts made a mistake on a coin from a new press, which had just come out and which they could not have known.
steps.simpleTranslation: They made a mistake about a coin from a new press, at the very time it was coming out of the press.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the experts got a brand-new coin wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A coin from a new press had never been seen before, so even the best expert could not know it. This is why the top expert is exempt: his mistake was not from missing knowledge.

keyTerms.meaning: a new press or stamp for making coins

steps.whatToRemember: A top expert is exempt only when he could not have known, like with a brand-new coin. A regular expert who errs must pay.

phrases.english: They made a mistake about a coin from a new press,
at the very time it was coming out from under the press.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 32.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They erred on a coin from a brand-new press that no one had seen yet.

steps.title: רבי חייא swaps a bad coin he approved
steps.stepSummary: A woman showed רבי חייא a coin, and he said it was good. The next day she said others called it bad and she could not spend it. רבי חייא told רב to exchange it for her and write it down as a bad deal.
steps.simpleTranslation: A woman showed a dinar to רבי חייא. He told her it was good. The next day she came back and said: I showed it to others, they told me it is bad, and I cannot spend it. He told רב: Go exchange it for her, and write in my notebook: 'This was a bad deal.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about a great sage who said a coin was good and it turned out bad.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story fits the money changer case just discussed. רבי חייא did not argue with the woman. He gave her a good coin in place of the bad one and had it written down as his own loss.

keyTerms.meaning: good, proper (a good coin)
bad
exchange it
notebook, record book

phrases.aramaic: הָהִיא אִיתְּתָא דְּאַחְזְיָא דִּינָרָא לְרַבִּי חִיָּיא,
phrases.english: A certain woman showed a dinar to רבי חייא,
he said to her: It is good.
The next day she came before him,
and said to him: I showed it to others,
and they told me it is bad,
and I cannot spend it!

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ לְרַב: זִיל חַלְּפֵיהּ נִיהֲלַהּ,
phrases.english: He said to רב: Go exchange it for her,
and write in my notebook:
'This was a bad deal.'

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהִיא אִיתְּתָא דְּאַחְזְיָא דִּינָרָא לְרַבִּי חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells a real story about the money changer case from steps 30-33.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי חייא, who approved a bad coin, gave the woman a good coin in its place and recorded it as a bad deal.

steps.title: Why did an expert like רבי חייא pay?
steps.stepSummary: If top experts like דנכו and איסור are exempt because they need no more learning, then רבי חייא, who was also such an expert, should have been exempt too.
steps.simpleTranslation: What makes דנכו and איסור different, so that they are exempt? It is because they don't need to learn anything more. But רבי חייא didn't need to learn anything more either!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the story of רבי חייא. He was a top expert, so by the rule we just learned he should not have had to pay. Why did he pay?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 31 said a top expert is exempt because he needs no more training. רבי חייא fits that description exactly. So the rule and the story seem to clash: an expert who should be exempt acted as if he owed money.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? (asks why one case is treated differently from another)
They are exempt (they don't have to pay)
To learn (here: to learn more about judging coins)
Also, too

phrases.english: And what is different about Dankhu and Issur
that they are exempt? It is because they do not need to learn.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי חִיָּיא נָמֵי לָאו לְמִיגְמַר קָא בָּעֵי!
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya too did not need to learn!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets the story of רבי חייא (step 34) against the rule exempting top experts (step 31).
steps.kashyaTarget: The story in step 34, where רבי חייא made good on the bad coin.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By the reason in step 31, a top expert who needs no more learning is exempt. רבי חייא was such an expert, so he should not have had to pay.

steps.title: רבי חייא went beyond the letter of the law
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא really was exempt. He paid only because he chose to act לפנים משורת הדין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא was acting beyond the letter of the law.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The rule still stands; רבי חייא simply chose to give more than the law required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer does not change the rule that a top expert is exempt. It explains that the story shows extra goodness, not legal duty. So there is no clash between the rule and the story.

keyTerms.meaning: Beyond the line of the law: doing more than the law strictly requires
That he did (acted)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think this means top experts must pay after all. The law still exempts them. רבי חייא paid by his own choice.
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that a person can be legally free and still be praised for going beyond the law. That is the point of the source the גמרא brings next.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי חִיָּיא, לִפְנִים מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין הוּא דַּעֲבַד.
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya acted beyond the letter of the law.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי חִיָּיא, לִפְנִים מִשּׁוּרַת הַדִּין הוּא דַּעֲבַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the story: the payment was voluntary, not required by law.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רבי חייא paid because the law made him pay, which would contradict the exemption for top experts.
steps.terutzMaskana: He was legally exempt. He paid only as an act of going beyond the law.

steps.title: רב יוסף's teaching on "and you shall show them"
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts bringing רב יוסף's teaching on a פסוק as the source for acting לפנים משורת הדין.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what רב יוסף taught: "And you shall show them" — this refers to...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is backing up its answer with a ברייתא taught by רב יוסף. The quote begins here and continues in the next part of the text.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף reads the פסוק in שמות 18:20 word by word, giving each phrase its own lesson. One of those lessons will turn out to be acting לפנים משורת הדין. So far we only have the first words of the פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: As was taught (introduces a teaching from a ברייתא)
And you shall show them (שמות 18:20)
This (means / refers to)

phrases.english: As Rav Yosef taught:
"And you shall show them" — this refers to
phrases.notes: שמות 18:20. The sentence keeps going in the next part of the text.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to support the answer in step 36.
steps.raayaObject: The idea of acting לפנים משורת הדין.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב יוסף's teaching on the פסוק "וְהוֹדַעְתָּ לָהֶם" (שמות 18:20), which continues in the next part of the text.
